summary: The note explains impeachment in the United States, covering both state-level and federal procedures. Impeachment is the lower house bringing charges against a civil officer, analogous to a grand jury indictment, while the upper house conducts the trial. It notes that at least eleven state governors have faced impeachment trials, with the most recent being Rod Blagojevich of Illinois in 2009, and summarizes the federal constitutional provisions and the Supreme Court's ruling in Nixon v. United States (1993).
one_line: Explains how U.S. impeachment works at state and federal levels, including the role of each house and notable governor impeachments.
key_facts: In New York, the Assembly impeaches and the State Senate tries the case, with the seven-judge New York State Court of Appeals members sitting with the senators as jurors.
At least eleven U.S. state governors have faced an impeachment trial.
Governor Lee Cruce of Oklahoma escaped impeachment conviction by a single vote in 1912.
Connecticut's John G. Rowland resigned rather than face impeachment when events seemed to make it inevitable.
On January 14, 2009, the Illinois House of Representatives voted 117 - 1 to impeach Rod Blagojevich on corruption charges.
The Illinois Senate removed Rod Blagojevich from office and barred him from holding future office on January 29, 2009.
Rod Blagojevich was the eighth U.S. state governor to be removed from office.
Impeachment in the United States is the process by which the lower house of a legislature brings charges against a civil officer, analogous to an indictment by a grand jury.
Most impeachments concern alleged crimes committed while in office, though a few officials were impeached and convicted for prior crimes.
The impeached official remains in office until a trial is held, and removal upon conviction is separate from the impeachment itself.
At the federal level, the House of Representatives has the sole power of impeaching.
The United States Senate has the sole power to try all impeachments.

Article Two, Section 4 of the United States Constitution states that the President, Vice President, and all civil Officers shall be removed on impeachment for and conviction of Treason, Bribery, or other High Crimes and Misdemeanors.
The removal of impeached federal officials is automatic upon conviction in the Senate.
In Nixon v. United States (1993), the Supreme Court determined that the federal judiciary cannot review such proceedings.
